This can expose sensitive host files and can stage command execution that runs when the user later starts a build of an execution environment. Preconditions: the extension is installed and the agent processes attacker-influenced content. The record lists a local attack vector, no privileges and user interaction required.

An MCP server that supplies local files to an agent offers a read tool taking a caller-supplied path. The path is resolved against the working directory and checked for accessibility without enforcing project containment. An attacker who can invoke the endpoint or tool can therefore read files outside the intended project wherever the server process has filesystem permission. Exploitation also requires that no effective runtime policy strip or constrain the supplied values before they reach the file operation. The record lists a network attack vector, no privileges and no user interaction. The reporter describes a caller invoking the tool directly.

A gateway project includes a separate sandbox server that executes caller-supplied code in a restricted environment. Its exposed attribute-access capabilities and incomplete validation let submitted code escape those restrictions and run operating-system commands with the server process's privileges. An attacker must be able to submit code to this sandbox server. Its HTTP-based transports can expose the execution tool without authentication; standard-input deployments retain the vulnerable execution path but reduce network exposure. Container host mounts and internal-network access can increase the resulting impact. The core gateway and proxy are not directly affected. The record lists network access, no privileges and no user interaction. The attacker submits code directly.

An MCP server that forwards an agent's requests to a local text-generation backend accepts an API base address as an argument of many tools. The address is not restricted to the intended backend, so the server can be made to send requests to loopback, private-network, cloud metadata or attacker-controlled hosts from its own network position. The reporter's issue describes the attacker as an MCP caller. The advisories say the attack can be launched on the local host. The record lists a local attack vector, low privileges required and no user interaction. The caller supplies the address directly.

A plugin for a website content-management system connects the site to AI agents through an MCP server. It has an access control flaw that lets a user with a contributor-level account do more than that role allows. The advisories do not name the affected function or describe the impact further, and state no other precondition. The record lists a network attack vector, low privileges required and no user interaction. The sources do not say who supplies the input.

A code generator for API clients and AI assistant plugins copies template file references from extension fields in an API description into a generated plugin manifest without validating their location. One extension path propagates the supplied reference only when a title is present; another copies the template reference directly. An attacker-controlled description can therefore make the deployed assistant host resolve files outside the plugin package. The flaw does not execute code on the build machine. Preconditions include generating the relevant plugin type from a malicious or compromised description and deploying the result; the demonstrated setup enables preview features. The record lists network access, no privileges and no user interaction. The attacker supplies the description document directly.

A client library for MCP supports credentials in custom HTTP headers. Its default HTTP client follows cross-origin redirects and removes standard credential headers while forwarding custom ones, potentially sending API keys or tokens to an attacker-controlled destination. Preconditions include using the streamable HTTP transport with the default redirect behavior and putting secrets in custom headers. The attacker must control the endpoint's redirect response, through a malicious or compromised server or a network position capable of altering that response. The separate standard authentication-header mechanism is unaffected. The record lists network access, high attack complexity, no privileges and no user interaction. The attacker supplies the redirect directly.

A client library for MCP reads server-sent event streams over HTTP and appends incoming data to a memory buffer that is cleared only when an event separator arrives. There is no size limit, so a server that keeps streaming without ever sending the separator makes the client's memory grow until the process crashes. Preconditions: the client uses the HTTP transport, and the server it connects to is malicious or compromised, or someone on the network path can alter a plaintext response. The CVE record lists a network attack vector, no privileges and active user interaction; the global advisory lists no user interaction. The input comes directly from that server or network party.

A server library for MCP manages sessions over HTTP streaming transports but does not check that requests using a session identifier come from the client that owns the session. Anyone holding another user's session identifier can call tools within that session, and the results are delivered to the victim's stream, so the victim may take them as genuine. The precondition is that the attacker has obtained a valid session identifier; the source treats how as out of scope. The record lists a network attack vector, attack requirements present, no privileges and no user interaction. The attacker sends requests directly.

A server library for MCP allocates an in-memory session before completing initialization checks and fails to remove the allocation when those checks reject the request. An attacker directly supplies otherwise well-formed protocol requests that reach session creation but fail initialization validation. Repetition permanently grows the session table for the process's lifetime, exhausting memory and delaying legitimate operations. Preconditions are the stateful streamable HTTP transport, the in-memory session manager and access to the listener. The advisory describes local processes as attackers under the default allowed-host configuration, and network attackers when the deployment permits their access. The record lists a network attack vector, no privileges and no user interaction.

A client library for connecting agents to tool services caches identity tokens without separating them by intended audience. When an application authenticates to multiple audiences in one process, a valid, unexpired token issued for one service can be reused in a request to another. An attacker who operates, compromises or monitors traffic to the receiving service can capture the token and replay it against its intended service to impersonate the application. Preconditions include multiple audiences sharing the process and a reusable token remaining valid. The application's requests trigger the cache mistake; the source describes attacker receipt and replay, without identifying attacker-supplied input that triggers the initial reuse. The record lists network access, additional attack requirements, no privileges and no user interaction.

An agent development toolkit runs a coding agent in a sandbox and relays tool calls to tools exposed by the host. The relay accepts requests from any process whose command line contains an allowed helper script path, so code running in the sandbox can call host tools, such as secret lookups, deployments and cloud operations, without a matching tool call from the model. Preconditions: hosts whose per-process information is read from the process filesystem (the vulnerable fallback runs only there), an active session with host-provided tools, and untrusted code running in the sandbox, such as a malicious dependency, build script or lifecycle hook. The record lists a local attack vector, no privileges and no user interaction. That code sends the relay requests directly.
